title: Orsen and the Postcards
premise: Quentin Dravenmoor, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word, returns to her family's condemned house to settle the estate before demolition. Behind a wardrobe she finds a box of undelivered postcards written by her grandmother in that dying language — letters addressed to a lover Quentin never knew existed. As she translates them against the demolition deadline, she uncovers how duty silenced love for three generations, including her own almost-confession to a woman named Orsen. In the end, Quentin delivers the final postcard by hand, speaks the untranslatable sentence aloud in the half-remembered tongue, and chooses truth over inheritance by letting the house fall.
about_author: Rosalind Ashgrove is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered correspondence in municipal storage. She writes about language, houses, and the things families seal behind walls.

chapters.title: The Word That Won't Stay
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Working on a commercial translation in her city flat, Quentin reaches for a childhood word and finds it gone — the third loss this month. Her editor calls about the Dravenmoor house: demolition in six weeks unless she signs papers. Emotional beat: quiet dread of erasure, both linguistic and architectural.

chapters.title: Return to Ashgrove Lane
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She arrives at the shuttered family house, dusty and scheduled for the wrecking ball, where a neighbor mentions her grandmother never let anyone into the back bedroom. Quentin sleeps badly in her childhood room. Emotional beat: the uncanny pull of a place that remembers more than she does.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Moving the wardrobe to measure the wall, she finds a cavity holding a tin box: forty-one postcards, all addressed to an 'E. Voss,' none stamped, all in the fading language. The first one she can still read. Emotional beat: vertigo — history cracking open under her hands.

chapters.title: A Grammar of Longing
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, with translated excerpts. She begins translating at the kitchen table, discovering her grandmother Maren wrote to E. Voss for nine years — tender, funny, increasingly desperate letters. Some words defeat her; she invents around them. Emotional beat: intimacy with a grandmother she thought she knew.

chapters.title: Orsen
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A woman appears at the gate asking if the house is really coming down — Orsen Voss, granddaughter of E. Voss, holding one stamped postcard that did get delivered decades ago. Emotional beat: recognition like a struck bell; Quentin realizes E. Voss was a man who loved her grandmother back.

chapters.title: What the Family Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Quentin present-day, Maren in 1968 via letter fragments. Quentin confronts her mother's old friend, learning Maren married Quentin's grandfather three months after E. Voss left town — an arrangement of property and respectability. Emotional beat: anger hardening into grief.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Postcard nineteen contains a sentence Quentin cannot render — its grammar exists only in the dying language, expressing a vow between staying and leaving simultaneously. She copies it out and stares at it for hours. Emotional beat: frustration curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, flashback-heavy. We learn of Orsen-the-younger — no, of Quentin's own almost-said confession to a college friend named Ilse, abandoned for career and safety. The parallel with Maren becomes unbearable. Emotional beat: shame surfacing after long burial.

chapters.title: Inventory of a House
chapters.summary: Quentin and Orsen's POV alternating. Orsen helps Quentin catalogue the house for the estate sale; they find E. Voss's carved initials inside the wardrobe itself. Tension rises as the demolition notice is posted on the gate. Emotional beat: two strangers building trust over shared ruins.

chapters.title: Postcards Twenty-Two Through Thirty
chapters.summary: Maren's voice dominates through translation. The letters turn practical — money enclosed, requests for silence — revealing Maren funded E. Voss's exile to protect him from her husband's family. Emotional beat: love expressed as logistics, devotion disguised as paperwork.

chapters.title: The Cousin Arrives
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Her cousin Aldous arrives demanding she sign the demolition consent immediately; he suspects the house holds valuables and begins searching rooms himself. Quentin hides the box. Emotional beat: the machinery of inheritance turning predatory.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Quentin and Orsen's POV. At Orsen's urging, Quentin reads a postcard aloud in the old language and finds her fluency returning — speech unlocking memory. But she stumbles on the untranslatable sentence again and refuses to guess. Emotional beat: tentative joy shadowed by what remains unsayable.

chapters.title: E. Voss's Side
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen shares her grandfather's diary: he waited eleven years for a reply that never came, not knowing Maren's letters were intercepted by Quentin's grandfather. Emotional beat: heartbreak of crossed wires across a generation.

chapters.title: Aldous Finds the Tin
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Aldous discovers the box and threatens to sell the postcards as 'family ephemera' to a dealer, arguing the past has market value only. Quentin physically bars the door. Emotional beat: open conflict; loyalty to the dead versus greed among the living.

chapters.title: The Interception Letter
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In her grandfather's study desk she finds proof: his own confession note admitting he burned Maren's replies and kept E. Voss's letters undelivered. The whole tragedy was maintenance of respectability. Emotional beat: cold clarity; the villain was duty itself.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Permits move up the demolition date by four days. Aldous files a claim on the postcards; Quentin photographs every card as insurance and drafts a legal challenge she may not win. Emotional beat: clock ticking, allies chosen.

chapters.title: Translating the Sentence
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, night scene. Alone in the kitchen, Quentin finally renders the untranslatable sentence: 'I stay so you may leave, and leave so you may stay' — a vow that holds contradiction without resolving it. She understands Maren completely, and herself. Emotional beat: breakthrough, devastating and calm.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Quentin and Aldous's POV. At the county office, Quentin argues the postcards are cultural material warranting preservation delay; Aldous argues private property. She loses the legal point but wins a five-day reprieve on a technicality. Emotional beat: costly, partial victory.

chapters.title: Delivery
chapters.summary: Quentin and Orsen's POV. Quentin hand-delivers the entire box to Orsen at E. Voss's restored workshop, completing the delivery twelve years — and fifty years — late. They read the final postcard together. Emotional beat: ceremony, restitution, tears neither apologizes for.

chapters.title: Ilse's Number
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin calls Ilse, says the sentence she withheld twelve years ago — plainly, in plain language this time. Ilse is quiet, then honest: too much time, but thank you. Emotional beat: release without reward; truth as its own inheritance.

chapters.title: The House Comes Down
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Quentin, Orsen, and a small crowd watch the excavators take the house. Quentin signs nothing further; Aldous gets his sale but not the postcards, which are donated to the regional archive under both names. Emotional beat: grief and relief in the same breath.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, epistolary coda. Months later, Quentin compiles a personal glossary of the dying language, beginning with the untranslatable sentence, and mails a copy to Orsen. The last entry is a new word she coins herself. Emotional beat: quiet hope — languages die, but meaning can be carried forward by hand.
